sections.text: Arjuna argued: My Lord! How can I, when the battle rages, send an arrow through Bheeshma and Drona, who should receive my reverence?

Rather would I content myself with a beggars crust than kill these teachers of mine, these precious noble souls! To slay these masters who are my benefactors would be to stain the sweetness of lifes pleasures with their blood.
Nor can I say whether it were better that they conquer me or for me to conquer them, since I would no longer care to live if I killed these sons of Dhritarashtra, now preparing for fight.

We will be discussing chapter two, Sankhya Yoga. Yoga of Knowledge means uniting with the knowledge. The knowledge can be generally classified into two categories. One is secular knowledge and sacred. Secular is the knowledge about the world of objects. So even to get the secular knowledge, what we generally have to do is to make observations of the objects and then understand them.
So all the objects in the world which we know about today are not dependent on my personal observation, my personal understanding. Generations of scientists, mathematicians, and experimenters have gathered this information and passed them to us. So our knowledge is based on the efforts of generations of great thinkers. Sacred knowledge is something similar. The knowledge about the self is also not my personal experience right now; I have to depend on the generations of sages who very carefully contemplated on the nature of the self.
And those declarations are basically recorded in Vedas in our tradition. The knowledge they gained in their contemplation, in their observation, in their meditations are recorded as declarations in the Vedas. Veda comes from vid, to know -- so the Vedas are literally the books of knowledge. So there are four Vedas, Rukh, Sam, Yajur and Atharva. Based on the declarations of Vedas, there are six Darshan Shastras in our traditions. Various masters have taken those declarations and formulated a school of philosophy to explain the truth, the nature of the self.
And that became the six schools of philosophy. In our tradition they can be generally categorized into three main categories. The first is called Tarka Logic. They come to the conclusion about what the truth is by logical conclusions. So thats called Tarka. And there are two great masters, Kannada and Gautam.
They formed their Darsana Sastra, which are called Vaisheshika and Nyaya. Out of the six schools, five of them do not believe that God can be realized by meditation and knowledge. Only the last one, Vedanta, recognized the fact that God can be realized by meditation and knowledge. So as I said, they can be classified into three categories. The first is Tarka, which is logic. Second is Sankhya, which is the logical enumeration of the facts.
Very logical argument about what is the truth and how we come to that conclusion. And Kapil Muni is the author of Sankhya philosophy. But he did not include the Creator Ishvara or the God Principle in his philosophy. So his Darshan Sastra is Nir-Ishwara -- Ishwara is not included in his thesis. But then Patanjali included Isvara in the same Sankhya philosophy.
So it becomes Sa-Ishwara Sankhya. The last category is called Mimamsa -- deliberations. Deliberating the facts which are available to us and coming to the conclusion of what is the real truth. So the declarations in Vedas are in basically two general categories. The earlier part of Vedas is called Karmakanda. The later part of the Vedas called Jnanakanda. The deliberations made based on the earlier part of the Vedas is called Purva Mimsa.
Jaimini Rishi made his treatise on this Purva Mimamsa -- a methodical path of how to achieve the ultimate goal. The ultimate goal in Purva Vimansa is to go to heaven. All the good deeds and good rituals -- when you perform them and acquire merits (Punya), then you are given a place to experience happiness and peace and bliss. And that state is called Swarga. So the goal of life as per Purva Mimamsa is to achieve Swarga. Now, based on the Jnanakanda --
The later part of the Vedas, the Darsam Shastra which was developed by Sage Badarayan is called Uttar Mimansa. The Uttar Mimamsa is the one that recognized the one single entity, Brahman. Various teachers and Acharyas have taken the basis from one or the other of Darshana Shastra and created the schools of thoughts in our culture. And they are basically three Dvaita, the dualistic school. God and I are two different entities. They will never become one.
God is the Master and I am his servant. Madhvacharya founded this dualistic school of thought. Ramanujacharya established Visisht Advaita which says God is the whole and I am a part of Him. So most of our Vaishnava Sampradha is based on Vishist Advaita. Then the last one is Adhvaita. Bhagavan Shankaracharya established the school of thought called Advaita based on Vedanta. Vedanta literally means end of Vedas. At the end of the Vedas we have the Upanishads, whose declarations say that myself and God are one and the same. Tattvamasi that thou art, that which I am seeking is none other than my own self. That school is called Advaita philosophy, non dualistic school of thought. People have seen the Bhagavad Gita from all these different points of view. In our tradition -- the Chinmaya Mission tradition, or Shankaracharyas tradition -- we typically look at it from the non-dualistic school of thought. This chapter combines all these various schools of thought into an understandable philosophy, taking the salient points of all three.
But in nature this chapter is still Advaitic. And therefore we have the saying in Sanskrit that the Gita rains the nectar of Advaita, which teaches us that myself and Gods self are one and the same. So therefore this chapter is titled Sankhya Yoga, Yoga of Knowledge, predominantly based on the Sankhya philosophy of logical conclusions. So it is more scientific and modern in its approach towards the truth. All our Upanishads are in the form of dialogues between student and the teacher. The student asks a question, and the teacher answers or gives guidance. So it is never to be taken without any understanding. If you dont understand, ask questions. Bhagavad Gita is basically in the same format. Bhagavan gives advice Arjuna, if he does not understand, he stops him and says let me tell you what I dont understand. So thats the tradition where you do not take anything for granted without understanding it.
So Chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga, is now giving us a thumbnail picture of the core declarations in the Vedas. In modern-day presentation, effective communication generally has three parts: tell them what youre going to tell them, then tell them, and then tell them what you told them. You go to any professional meeting -- you have an agenda. You tell them what were going to discuss today, then you hold a discussion on those items, and at the end of the meeting you conclude with action items and what we agreed on.
So that tradition is started by Bhagawan Vedvyasan, not our marketing guru. So chapter two will tell us what we will be discussing throughout Bhagavad Gita. Then well be discussing Bhagavad Gita and Chapter 18 will tell us what we discussed all throughout Bhagavad Gita -- the conclusion, the action items, what we have to do now after having learned Bhagavad Gita. So the Sankhya Yoga is yoga of knowledge. Assuming that I dont have the knowledge right now, therefore Im going to learn.
So chapter one gave us the scenario of our life situations. We typically live our life by complaining about injustices, discriminations, unfairness. And therefore what we do is we try to prepare ourselves for overcoming those obstacles. Thats what we call education, training, internships. These are basically our preparations. Now is the preparation good enough to achieve success and happiness in life?
Theres something more. All the graduates who come out from the university, they dont achieve exactly the same results. Theyre all prepared with similar training, yet they dont achieve the same results. Why? Because there is something else where they differ from each other -- their inner strength, inner qualities, and inner understandings of how to deal with situations.
When you encounter a situation, will you be able to take the right decision? What to do and what not to do is basically the training in the spiritual quest. If we have the clear understanding about what my position is in this situation and what my role is in this situation, then Ill be able to take the decision correctly. If I represent a company, when I go to a meeting with my client, if I have clear understanding what my role is as a company employee, then what my goal is here, then I will take the right decision. But if I misunderstand my role and introduce my personal objectives and personality into that discussion, then I as a company representative will fail. I actually never get chances to be on a selection side of an interview.
Typically Im more a candidate for pitching our services to other people. Once in a while I get an opportunity to be on a selection site to interview contractors. And I just had one interview like that. And after the three or four candidates we interviewed were obviously sitting down and making selections. So there were four or five people in that room. And you can tell that some people are completely unbiased and they really have no extra grind.
But then there are some people who say, yeah, but I know that guy and I like him. So Im now injecting my personal bias into the decision making process. If you take that personal bias out of it, your decision will be relatively correct. But once you start seeing it through your personal bias, your decision will be deluded. May or may not be correct. So what we have seen in chapter one is when your personal attachments and biases are overwhelming you in facing the situation, the chances of your failure is much greater.
So you have seen the Arjuna when he was part of the Pandavas army as a general, he was very enthusiastic and very, very confident about his ability to fight. But as soon as he starts seeing other people as his relatives, he basically introduced his own attachment to them and thats where he got confused and broken down. So that was the scenario of the first chapter, basically gave us a mirror to our own situation why we fail in some situation and we succeed in other situations. The situations where I was overwhelmed by my own attachment and biases, it did not let me take the right decision. Situation where I have kept myself out of personal biases and saw the situation through a correct lens. If I was a part of a community, part of a country, as a citizen, or a part of a company, as a company representative, I take the right decision.
So chapter two obviously starts with continuation of the dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna. Mainly Arjuna spoke about himself. Krishna has not said anything. Sanjay has been narrating it to Dhritarashtra. So Chapter 2 starts with Sanjaya reporting back to Dhritarashtra -- Tam Tatha Krupaya Avistam -- simply reporting to Dhritarashtra that this is what Krishna said to Arjuna. Because it may be possible that listening to Arjuna, Dhrutrashtra may have developed some hope that I think this is going to be the end of it.
I think Arjuna is going to convince Krishna to lets pack our bags and go home. And when Arjuna is not there, either they all will go back or even if they fight, they are not going to win without Arjuna. So Dhritarasra may have some hope that the strategy is working. Arjuna is now broken down completely in this psychological warfare between what is right and wrong. Our emissaries went there, their emissaries came here. We put our argument, they put theirs -- we won over Arjuna.
So Sanjay says, wait a minute, let me tell you what Krishna told him. Tam Tatha Tam to him Tatha Das Krupaya Avistam. He is describing Arjunas condition. Krupaya Avistam is overwhelmed by pity. Ashra Purna is crying. Can you imagine a general in the army on the battlefield, ready to fight, crying.

Arjunas anguish in these verses reflects a universal human dilemma: How can I act against those I revere and love, even when duty demands it? He protests that he would rather beg for food than enjoy pleasures stained with the blood of his teachers Bhishma and Drona. This is not mere sentimentality - it is the voice of deep moral conflict. Yet notice how Arjunas reasoning, though emotionally compelling, is fundamentally self-centered: How can I fight them? I would no longer care to live if I killed them.
Today, examine your own life for similar conflicts where you rationalize inaction because taking right action seems too painful. Perhaps it is a difficult conversation you avoid with a family member, a professional boundary you fear to set, or a truth you hesitate to speak. Like Arjuna, we often dress up our fears in noble-sounding arguments. We say I cannot hurt them when we really mean I cannot bear the discomfort of this situation.
Ask yourself: Where in my life am I using respect or love as an excuse to avoid my responsibilities? What begging for food - settling for less than I am capable of - am I willing to accept rather than face a necessary challenge? Remember, the pleasures we enjoy while avoiding our duty are indeed stained with blood - the blood of our own unfulfilled potential.
